meta.blurb: Prince Felix is days from an arranged engagement, so he catches a night train and vanishes. In a lakeside bookshop he becomes plain Fen, a terrible shop assistant, until a festival of lanterns and a newspaper change everything.
meta.bible: Felix: Crown Prince of Aldoria, twenty-six, polite, clever and never allowed to choose; calls himself Fen in Lindenmere. King Anton: Felix's father, stern, secretly a romantic; his late wife, Felix's mother, once sold apple pies in a market. Livia: Felix's sister, a princess of seventeen, clever and brave. Lady Cecile Marchand: Felix's intended bride, who loves another man, the stable master. Captain Hale: the kind old head of the palace guard. Maren Vos: owner of the Lantern Bookshop, practical and warm; her father opened the shop and has died. Pepper: the shop cat. Mrs Kell: the grumpy baker of Lindenmere who has a good heart. Nina Strand: a newspaper reporter. Aldoria: a mountain kingdom. Halden Palace: the palace in Aldoria. Brinmark: the neighbouring country. Lindenmere: a small lake town in Brinmark. The Lantern Bookshop: the shop with a green door, a debt to the bank due by the end of October. The Night of Lanterns: the book festival by the lake. The Harvest Ball: the court ball where the engagement is to be announced. The Royal Reading Fund: Felix and Livia's plan for village libraries. Voice and tone: warm, funny and romantic; a gentle comedy of a prince learning to be ordinary, with a happy ending.

B1B2: Prince Felix of Aldoria stood at his window and watched the gardeners prepare for the Harvest Ball. In six weeks his engagement would be announced to the whole kingdom.
That morning King Anton explained, kindly but firmly, that the match with Lady Cecile was good for the kingdom. Felix tried to speak, but he had never learned how to disagree with a king.
Princess Livia, who was seventeen and very clever, found him in the library that evening. She put a plain coat and a train ticket in his hands and said that he should go.
Just before midnight Felix crept down the back stairs in his plain coat and cap. The cook was asleep in her chair, and nobody saw the prince of Aldoria slip out into the night.
The night train rattled through the mountains, and Felix sat alone by the window. When the ticket inspector asked his name, he said the first one that came into his head, which was Fen.

At dawn the train reached Lindenmere, a small town on a misty lake in the neighbouring country of Brinmark. Felix had never bought anything with his own money, and he stood in the street holding a handful of strange coins.
On a narrow street he found the Lantern Bookshop, with a crooked sign in the window. It said that the shop needed an assistant, and Felix, who needed a hiding place, went inside.
A young woman was standing on a tall ladder with an armful of books. This was Maren Vos, the owner, and she looked at the newcomer as if he were a very odd customer.
Maren asked what he could do, and Felix, to his own surprise, told the truth: almost nothing. She hired him for a week anyway, because she could not afford anyone better.
Felix had never carried anything heavier than a ceremonial sword, and the boxes of books were a shock. On his first morning he dropped one box, broke a teacup and sold a customer the wrong book.
At closing time Maren showed Felix a letter from the bank. The shop owed a lot of money, and unless she paid it by the end of October, the Lantern Bookshop would close for good.
On Saturday morning Maren asked Felix to read to the children in the shop. He had grown up being read to by tutors, so he did all the voices, and the children adored him.
That evening Felix tried to cook supper and burned everything, including the toast. Maren laughed until she cried, and then she showed him how to make soup, step by step.
Felix's room was a tiny attic under the roof, with a narrow bed and a window over the lake. It was smaller than his palace wardrobe, and he had never slept better.
Back in Aldoria, Captain Hale reported to the king that the prince had vanished. King Anton ordered a search, but he asked that it be kept secret from the newspapers.
One evening Maren told Felix about her father, who had read to her every night. He had died two years ago, and the shop was all that she had left of him.
Felix had an idea, and it came to him while he watched the lake. They could hold a festival of books at night, with lanterns along the water and every shop in town joining in.
They named it the Night of Lanterns and began to plan every detail. Felix, who had been taught to draw by a very strict teacher, made posters so beautiful that Maren could hardly believe it.
Together they visited every shop in Lindenmere to ask for help. Mrs Kell the baker was the hardest to convince, but Felix charmed her with a bow and promised to carry her flour.

One night a storm knocked out the lights, so Maren lit candles in the shop. They sat on the floor among the books, and Felix told her how he really felt about nearly everything, though not who he was.
Felix, who had always been good at sums, went through Maren's money books one night. He found that the shop lost money on slow old stock, and he drew her a plan to fix it.
A newspaper reporter named Nina Strand arrived to write about the festival. She took photographs of the shop, the lake and the cheerful new assistant, who tried to hide behind a shelf.
That night Livia called him from the palace, speaking in a whisper. Lady Cecile also wanted to end the engagement, she said, but she needed Felix to be brave first.
Felix lay awake all night, because he knew that he could not hide forever. Yet he did not want to leave Maren, the shop or the festival that was almost ready.
In the last week before the festival, the whole of Lindenmere joined in the work. Bakers made cakes, children painted lanterns, and the man who mended umbrellas built a stage out of old doors.
On the last evening Maren and Felix hung the final lanterns along the shore. When her ladder wobbled, Felix caught her, and for a moment neither of them moved.
On the night of the festival, the first visitors arrived at dusk. By eight o'clock the lanes were full, and hundreds of lanterns glowed along the dark water.
Maren asked Felix to read the opening story from the little stage. His voice carried across the water, and the crowd listened in perfect silence until the last line.
By midnight the Lantern Bookshop had sold nearly every book on its shelves. When Maren counted the money, she realised that the shop had earned almost everything it owed the bank.
When the crowds had gone, Maren and Felix walked out onto the little wooden bridge. Under a hundred glowing lanterns, she turned to him and kissed him first.
The next morning they ate toast together, and Felix burned it only a little. Maren asked him to stay for good, and for a moment he forgot that he had a kingdom.
Before lunch, Nina Strand's article appeared in the newspaper, with a large photograph on the front page. It said that the missing prince of Aldoria had been found working in a bookshop.
Maren looked up from the page and asked him if it was true. Felix could have lied again, but he was tired of lying, so he told her everything.
Maren said that he had listened to her talk about her father while he hid his whole life from her. Felix said that he had been afraid that she would only see a prince.
Maren said that she needed time, and that Felix needed to decide who he really wanted to be. She asked him to go back to Aldoria and decide, and not to come back until he knew.
Outside, Captain Hale was waiting beside a black car at the end of the lane. He was a kind old soldier who had known Felix since he was a boy, and he did not say a word of blame.
As the car drove away, Felix looked back at the lantern ribbons still hanging by the lake. Then the mountains of Aldoria rose ahead of them, and his stomach turned over.
In the great hall King Anton told his son that the engagement would be announced as planned. For the first time in his life, Felix looked his father in the eye and said no.
The king said that a prince does not choose, but must do his duty. Felix answered that a prince who has never chosen anything has no idea what duty is for.
That night Felix met Livia and Lady Cecile in the library. They agreed that Cecile would speak first at the ball, and that Felix would stand beside her.
Late that night Felix sat down to write to Maren, and he threw away eleven pages. In the end he sent only a few lines, and a small parcel that he hoped she would open.
In Lindenmere, Maren opened the parcel and found a worn copy of her father's favourite book, the one she had lost years ago. The note said, “I never lied about the parts that mattered.”
A few days later a cream-coloured card arrived from Princess Livia, inviting Maren to the Harvest Ball. Maren almost threw it away, but Mrs Kell told her that she must go.
Maren travelled on the same night train that Felix had taken, wearing a dress that Mrs Kell had made. The mountains outside her window were so enormous that she felt as small as a button.

The Harvest Ball was held in a great hall of mirrors, with a thousand candles and an orchestra in the gallery. Felix stood by his father, pale and silent, waiting for the moment that Cecile had promised.
Before the king could speak, Lady Cecile stepped forward and said, in a clear voice, that she would not marry the prince. The whole court gasped, and a glass fell and broke.
Felix stepped forward and told the court that he agreed with Lady Cecile. He said he wanted to serve the kingdom by building libraries and schools, and by marrying only for love.
At that moment Felix saw Maren in the doorway, wearing a green dress and looking terrified. He crossed the whole hall without caring who watched, and stopped in front of her.
King Anton watched them across the hall, and his face slowly softened. He remembered the girl who had sold him an apple pie in the market, and how the court had said no to her too.

Months later, Felix arrived in Lindenmere every Saturday, wearing his old cap, to read to the children. The Lantern Bookshop was full of readers, the bank had been paid, and Maren no longer worried about the door.
C1C2: From his window high in Halden Palace, Prince Felix of Aldoria watched an army of gardeners hanging flowers for the Harvest Ball, and his heart sank lower with every garland. In six weeks the whole kingdom would hear that he was to marry Lady Cecile Marchand, whom he liked very much and did not love at all. He was twenty-six years old, and in all that time he had never once been allowed to decide anything for himself.

That morning his father, King Anton, explained in his calm, courteous voice that the match with Lady Cecile would bring peace, trade and a great deal of happiness to the kingdom. Felix opened his mouth to say that he was not sure it would bring any to him, but the words turned to dust, as they always did. He bowed, said that he understood, and left the room feeling like a parcel that had been signed for.

Princess Livia, who was seventeen and cleverer than the rest of the family together, found her brother in the library that evening, staring at nothing. She pushed a plain coat, a woollen cap and a train ticket into his hands and told him that nobody else was ever going to ask whether he was happy. He tried to protest, but she had already planned the whole escape on a sheet of paper, complete with arrows and a drawing of the kitchen door.

Just before midnight Felix crept down the servants' staircase in his borrowed coat, his shoes in his hand and his heart hammering against his ribs. The cook was snoring in her chair beside the great stove, and the sentry at the gate was busy with a sandwich, so that the heir to the throne of Aldoria walked out of his own home unseen. It was the first time in his life that he had gone through a door without someone opening it for him.

The night train rattled through the mountains and across the border, and Felix sat alone by the dark window, watching the last lights of his kingdom disappear. When the ticket inspector asked his name, he gave the first one that came into his head, a shortened scrap of his own, and it sounded surprisingly like a real person. Fen, he thought, could do anything, because nobody had ever told Fen what he was supposed to be.

At dawn the train sighed into Lindenmere, a small town of cobbled streets and crooked roofs on the edge of a misty lake in the neighbouring country of Brinmark. Felix stepped onto the platform with a handful of unfamiliar coins and no idea what any of them were worth, having never in his life bought anything for himself. He bought a bread roll, was charged far too much, and thought it the most exciting thing that had ever happened to him.

Halfway along a narrow lane he found the Lantern Bookshop, its green door propped open and a crooked, hand-painted sign in the window announcing that an assistant was wanted. Felix, who had no experience of work whatever but a pressing need of somewhere to hide, read the sign twice and felt that the universe was being unusually convenient. He straightened his borrowed coat, took a breath, and walked in to the jingle of a little bell.

A young woman was balanced on a tall ladder at the back of the shop, an armful of books held against her chest and a pencil stuck behind her ear. This was Maren Vos, the owner, and she studied the stranger in the doorway with the polite suspicion of someone who has been disappointed by applicants before. He had the posture of a soldier, the hands of a pianist and the haircut of a very expensive barber.

Maren asked what experience he had, and Felix, to his own astonishment, told the plain truth, which was almost none at all. She sighed, looked at the empty shop and the pile of unpaid bills beside the till, and offered him a week's trial and the small room above the stairs, since she could not afford anyone better. He shook her hand and promised himself that he would be the best assistant she had ever hired.

Felix had never carried anything heavier than a ceremonial sword, and the boxes of new books came as a shock to his arms and to his pride. During that first morning he dropped one box, broke a teacup, sold a customer a cookbook when she had asked for a thriller, and discovered that the till was a mystery he could not solve. Through all of it, Pepper the shop cat sat on the counter and watched him with narrow, unimpressed eyes.

When the last customer had gone, Maren showed Felix the letter from the bank that she had been carrying in her apron pocket for a week. The shop owed more than it could earn, it said, and unless the debt was paid by the end of October, the Lantern Bookshop would be closed and sold. Her father had opened it forty years ago, she said quietly, and she could not bear to be the person who locked its door for the last time.

On Saturday morning Maren, desperate for help with the weekly story hour, asked Felix to read to the children who crowded onto the rug. He had been taught elocution by the finest tutors in the kingdom, so he gave every dragon a rumbling growl and every princess a sharp tongue, and within minutes the whole room was spellbound. Maren, listening from behind the counter, forgot that she was supposed to be pricing a box of paperbacks.

That evening Felix announced that he would cook supper, and within ten minutes the kitchen was full of smoke, the toast was a pair of black tiles, and Pepper had fled to the roof. Maren laughed until she had to hold the table, then took the spoon from his hand and showed him how to make soup, one slow step at a time. It was the simplest meal he had ever eaten, and it was the best.

Felix's room turned out to be a tiny attic under the sloping roof, with a narrow iron bed, a crooked shelf and a window that looked out across the silver lake. It was smaller than the wardrobe he had left behind in Aldoria, and yet he lay awake for an hour in pure happiness, listening to the creak of the old building. Nobody knew where he was, and nobody was waiting for him to be somebody.

Back in Aldoria, the head of the palace guard, Captain Hale, stood before the king and reported, with great reluctance, that the prince had vanished in the night. King Anton, white with anger and something that looked suspiciously like fear, ordered a search at once, but insisted that it be kept secret from the newspapers and from the court. Only Livia sat calmly in the corner, turning the pages of a book she was not reading.

One evening, sitting on the shop steps with mugs of tea while the lake turned from silver to pewter, Maren told Felix about her father. He had read to her every night until she was old enough to read to him, and he had died two years ago. The shop, with its creaking floors and its smell of paper, was the only place where she could still hear his voice, and Felix, who had nothing wise to say, simply listened.

Felix's idea came to him as he watched the lamps being lit along the water, and it arrived so completely that he said it aloud before he had thought it through. They could hold a festival of books after dark, he said, with lanterns on the shore, readings under the trees and every shop in town taking part, and the crowds would pour in from all the villages around the lake. Maren stared at him for a long moment, and then she reached for a pencil.

They called it the Night of Lanterns, and for a week the shop was buried under maps, lists and cups of cold tea as they planned every detail. Felix, who had been taught to draw by a strict and rather terrifying teacher, produced posters so beautiful that Maren stopped in the street to stare at one pinned to a lamp post. She began, very slowly, to suspect that her new assistant was far cleverer than he let on.

Together they visited every shop in Lindenmere, from the cheesemonger to the man who mended umbrellas, asking each to join the festival with a stall or a lantern. Mrs Kell the baker was the hardest to persuade, being a woman who disapproved of nearly everything, but Felix gave her a bow so elegant and a smile so sincere that she agreed before she knew it. Outside, Maren whispered that she had never seen anyone win over Mrs Kell in under an hour.

One stormy night the lights went out all over Lindenmere, and Maren lit a dozen candles and set them among the shelves until the shop glowed like a cave of gold. They sat on the floor with a blanket across their knees while the rain drummed on the roof, and Felix found himself telling her what he truly felt about almost everything, though not who he was. For once, she did not interrupt, and the silence between his words was full of something that neither of them named.

Felix, who had always been good with numbers, spent a night going through Maren's account books and discovered that the shop was losing money on slow old stock while selling its best books too cheaply. He drew her a neat plan, with columns and arrows, that showed how a few small changes might save a good deal before the end of October. Maren looked at the page, then at him, and asked in a very odd voice where on earth he had learned to do that.

A newspaper reporter named Nina Strand arrived from the city to write a short piece about the festival, and she wandered the lanes with a notebook in one hand and a camera in the other. She photographed the shop, the lake and the cheerful new assistant, who tried to hide behind a rack of postcards and succeeded only in knocking it over. Nina looked at him a little longer than seemed polite, as though she were trying to remember something.

That night Livia telephoned him from the palace, whispering so quietly that Felix had to press the phone against his ear. Lady Cecile had been in love with someone else for years, she told him, and she was as relieved by his escape as she was frightened by the thought of facing the king alone. If Felix would only come home and say no, Cecile would say it too, and together they might break the whole arrangement.

Felix lay awake until the lake turned grey with morning, knowing that he could not hide in a bookshop for the rest of his life and that Cecile was waiting for his courage. Yet every time he imagined going home he saw Maren on her ladder with a pencil behind her ear, and the thought of leaving felt like cutting a thread that held his whole life together. He decided to wait until the festival was over, and told himself that the delay was merely sensible.

In the last week before the festival the whole of Lindenmere seemed to be working at once, as if the little town had woken from a long sleep. Bakers rolled out trays of honey cakes, children painted paper lanterns in every colour of the rainbow, and the man who mended umbrellas built a stage out of old doors and a great deal of cheerful grumbling. Even Mrs Kell, the grumpiest woman in the lane, was seen smiling at a lantern, though she denied it fiercely afterward.

On the last evening before the festival, Maren and Felix hung the final lanterns along the shore while the sky turned the colour of peaches. When her ladder wobbled, Felix caught her by the waist, and for a long moment the two of them stood so close that she could feel his heart racing as fast as her own. A dog barked somewhere, and they both stepped back with exaggerated interest in the nearest lantern.

On the night of the festival the first visitors arrived at dusk, in twos and threes, then in families, then in crowds that poured down every lane toward the lake. By eight o'clock the shore was a river of lights, with hundreds of paper lanterns glowing along the water and their reflections trembling in the dark. Maren stood at the door of her shop with her hand over her mouth, quite unable to speak.

At nine o'clock Maren asked Felix to read the opening story from the little stage, and he climbed up on legs that felt remarkably unreliable for a man who had once addressed a thousand dignitaries. His voice carried over the water, warm and unhurried, and the crowd listened in such complete silence that the lapping of the lake could be heard between the sentences. When he reached the last line, the applause rolled around the shore like thunder.

By midnight the Lantern Bookshop had sold nearly every book on its shelves, and the visitors were still queueing at the door with armfuls of paperbacks and eager faces. When Maren counted the takings at last, with Felix holding the lamp, she realised that, in a single night, the shop had earned almost everything it owed the bank. She sat down on the floor and laughed and cried at the same time.

When the last of the crowd had drifted home, Maren and Felix walked out onto the little wooden bridge, where the final lanterns were burning low over the black water. She turned to him, put both hands on his coat, and kissed him before either of them could think of a reason why they should not. The lake, the stars and one tired cat watching from the shop window were the only witnesses.

The next morning they ate breakfast on the shop steps, and Felix, who had improved with practice, burned the toast only a little. Maren asked him, shyly, whether he might consider staying for good, and for one golden moment he forgot that he had ever owned a kingdom, a palace or a secret. He said that there was nothing in the world he wanted more, which was true, and which also made the lie underneath it feel heavier than a mountain.

Before lunch, the newspaper that Nina Strand wrote for appeared in every shop in Lindenmere, and across its front page ran a photograph of Felix, laughing, with a book in his hand. The headline declared that the missing prince of Aldoria had been found, alive and well and working in a small bookshop beside a lake. Maren read it standing at the counter, and the colour drained slowly from her face.

Maren lowered the newspaper and asked him, in a voice so level that it frightened him, whether it was true. Felix could have invented one more story, but he was tired of lying to the only person who had ever liked him for his toast. So he told her everything: the palace, the engagement, the night train and the name he had borrowed from his own, while she listened to every word without once looking at him.

She told him, in a low and shaking voice, that he had let her talk about her father and her fears and her whole small world while he hid his own behind a cap and a false name. Felix said that he had been afraid, not that she would dislike the prince, but that she would stop seeing Fen, the only person he had ever been allowed to be. It was the truest thing he had ever said, and it did not help at all.

Maren said that she needed time, and that so did he, for a man who did not know whether he was a prince or a bookseller could not stand in her shop and be both. She asked him to go home, face whatever waited for him there, and decide who he truly wished to be before he came back, if he ever did. Then she turned toward the shelves so that he would not see her cry.

At the end of the lane Captain Hale was waiting beside a long black car, standing as straight as a post and holding his cap against his chest. He was a kind old soldier who had known Felix since the prince was a small boy with a toy sword, and he did not say a single word of blame. He only said that the king was asking for him, and that the road home was a long one.

As the car pulled away, Felix twisted around in his seat to watch the paper lanterns still hanging by the water, small and bright and getting smaller, until the lane bent and they were gone. By evening the great grey mountains of Aldoria rose ahead of them, as familiar as an old coat and as heavy as one too. He realised, with a strange calm, that he was no longer sure he was going home, because home had begun to mean something else.

In the great hall, with a dozen courtiers pretending not to listen, King Anton told his son in a voice like cold iron that the engagement would be announced exactly as planned, and that the escape would be forgotten. Felix, whose knees were not entirely steady, stood up straight, looked his father in the eye for the first time in his life, and said that he would not marry a woman he did not love. A silence fell that was so complete that a courtier's cough sounded like a crash.

The king, who was not accustomed to being contradicted, replied that a prince does not choose but serves, and that the kingdom had no room for the whims of a young man who read too many books. Felix answered, more gently than he had intended, that a prince who had never been allowed to choose anything could not truly understand what he was serving. The old man looked at him for a long time, and then, abruptly, he dismissed the court.

That night Felix met Livia and Lady Cecile in the library, where three candles burned low and a plan took shape. Cecile, who was brave in a quiet and unshakeable way, would speak first at the Harvest Ball and tell the court that she would not marry him, and Felix would stand at her side and say that he agreed. They shook hands on it solemnly, like conspirators, and Livia gave a small, triumphant bounce.

Late that night Felix sat at his desk to write to Maren, and he crumpled up eleven pages before he found words that were simple enough to be true. In the end he sent only a few lines, together with a small brown parcel that he had asked Captain Hale to find in the oldest bookshops of the capital. He did not expect an answer, but he found himself looking up every time a footstep passed his door, and he waited for one anyway.

In Lindenmere, Maren unwrapped the parcel at the counter and found a battered copy of her father's favourite book. It was the very one that had been lost when she was a child, and she had described it to Felix only once, on a stormy night. Tucked inside the cover was a note that read, “I never lied about the parts that mattered,” and she held it to her chest and smiled for the first time since the festival.

A few days later a thick cream-coloured card arrived from Princess Livia, inviting Maren to the Harvest Ball and promising, in a hasty postscript, that it would be worth the journey. Maren almost threw it in the stove, but Mrs Kell, who had come in to borrow a book and read it over her shoulder, informed her in no uncertain terms that she was going. By the end of the week, half the town had contributed something to her outfit.

Maren travelled on the same night train that Felix had taken, wearing a green dress that Mrs Kell had sewn with much grumbling and genuine skill. She pressed her forehead to the window as the mountains rose out of the dark, so vast and so old that she felt as small as a button. She wondered what it was like to be born into a kingdom that was also a cage, and she did not yet know what she would say to him.

The Harvest Ball was held in the great hall of mirrors, where a thousand candles multiplied themselves into a hundred thousand, and the orchestra played waltzes that the whole court knew by heart. Felix stood beside his father in his dress uniform, pale and silent, waiting for the moment that Cecile had promised and trying not to look at the doors. Then the king raised his hand for silence, and the great hall hushed as he prepared to announce the engagement of his son.

Before the king could speak, Lady Cecile stepped forward in her blue gown and said, in a voice that carried to every corner of the hall, that she loved another man and would not marry the prince. The court gasped as one, a glass fell and shattered on the marble, and the king's face turned the colour of old paper. Cecile curtsied deeply, took the arm of the stable master, who had been waiting among the servants, and walked out with her chin high.

Felix stepped forward into the astonished silence and said, as steadily as he could, that he agreed with Lady Cecile in every particular. He wished to serve Aldoria, he told them, not by being a handsome portrait on the palace wall, but by building libraries in every village and by marrying, if he ever married, only for love. When he finished, there was a silence so deep that the only sound in the whole hall was the spluttering of a single candle.

At that moment Felix noticed a figure in the great doorway, a young woman in a green dress, gripping her skirt in both hands and looking as though she might bolt. He crossed the whole length of the hall without caring who watched, and the crowd parted before him like water before the bow of a boat. He stopped in front of her and, for the first time that night, found that he had nothing prepared to say.

King Anton watched them across the hall for a long moment, and the stern lines of his face slowly gave way, like frost in the first sun. He remembered the girl who had once sold him an apple pie in the market, a girl the whole court had declared unsuitable, and who had become Felix's mother and the great love of his life. Then, to the amazement of everyone present, he raised his glass and said that the prince had his blessing.

Months later, the first of Felix's village libraries had opened in Aldoria, paid for by the Royal Reading Fund that he and Livia had founded. Every Saturday the prince himself arrived in Lindenmere in an old cap to read to the children, while the Lantern Bookshop filled with readers and the bank was repaid in full. A new sign over the green door welcomed readers of every kind, and Maren took his hand, understanding that some stories end well because someone was brave enough to begin.
